## Bi-Encoder vs Cross-Encoder

Now that we’ve established **derived reranking** as a precision-focused second pass and **hybrid reranking** as a recall-expanding fusion, it’s time to look at **how rerankers actually evaluate relevance**. At the core, most modern semantic rerankers fall into two camps: **bi-encoders** and **cross-encoders**. Each has a distinct philosophy and trade-off.

### Bi-Encoder

A **bi-encoder** is simply a siamese network, it independently encodes the query and the node/document into embeddings:

[![Cross-Encoders — Sentence Transformers documentation](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ef5V!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F641e55aa-6c8f-4901-a235-79786c69b837_226x267.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ef5V!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F641e55aa-6c8f-4901-a235-79786c69b837_226x267.png)

vq=encq(q),vd=encd(d)

Similarity is computed via cosine or dot product:

score(q,d)=cos⁡(vq,vd)

Intuition is simple, it is a pair-wise similarity search (but only on embedding level). Here, none of the embeddings are mixed or interact together (no cross-attention between query and node), the only place where they interact is score/similarity function (which is fixed):

- The query sends out a scout.

- Each node is represented in a pre-computed embedding space.

- Cosine similarity tells you roughly which nodes are close to your query.


**Strengths:**

- Extremely fast; embeddings can be precomputed.

- Scales to millions of nodes easily.


**Weaknesses:**

- Treats query and node independently; subtle relational cues (negation, token order, dependencies) are often lost.

- May rank semantically similar but contextually irrelevant nodes too high. example: “cats” vs “dogs” problem in legal or technical documents.


### Cross-Encoder

A **cross-encoder** feeds query and node together into a single model:

[![Cross-Encoders — Sentence Transformers documentation](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4jqj!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbf3ca255-f931-47f7-b3b6-e66e694d9e85_223x267.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4jqj!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbf3ca255-f931-47f7-b3b6-e66e694d9e85_223x267.png)

score(q,d)=fθ(\[q;d\])

Here, attention flows **across tokens** from both query and document, as the information is merged and shared into a single backbone for interaction/fusion. allowing the model to reason over relational and contextual nuances.

**Strengths:**

- Captures subtle distinctions like negation, qualifiers, multi-hop dependencies.

- Produces more accurate relevance scores for small candidate sets.


**Weaknesses:**

- Computationally expensive; embeddings cannot be precomputed.

- Not feasible to rerank millions of nodes directly.


### CoLBERT : Late Interaction as the Sweet Spot

We saw two scenarios, in Bi-encoder there was no interaction (hence fast) on the other hand we had Cross-encoder, where we had full/per-layer interaction (hence slow). Both are extremas for optimization. What if we had something in middle?

_**This is where CoLBERT elegantly finds the middle ground.**_ Instead of query level embeding (in Bi-encoder) or Query+Doc level embedding (in Cross-encoder),CoLBERT makes token level embeddings (chunks of query).

score(q,d)=∑i∈qmaxj∈dcos⁡(vqi,vdj)

**Intuition:**

- Each token in the query searches for its best match in the document.

- Token-level interactions provide _fine-grained reasoning_ like a mini-inspection.

- Yet, embeddings are computed independently, keeping inference _scalable_.


[![An Overview of Late Interaction Retrieval Models: ColBERT, ColPali, and  ColQwen | Weaviate](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!T-Fq!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9e14f3a9-44d8-4e36-ab29-377645f23c4b_1358x709.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!T-Fq!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9e14f3a9-44d8-4e36-ab29-377645f23c4b_1358x709.jpeg)

Colbert stands for Contextualized Late interaction over BERT. There are two key terms here. Contextualized we already know, but what does Late Interaction means?

Let’s formalize it.

Each query (which is broken at token level) and document is encoded by a shared encoder (e.g., BERT):

Q=\[q1,q2,...,qm\],D=\[d1,d2,...,dn\]

Each token embedding is _contextualized_, it knows its surroundings (thanks to BERT’s self-attention), but the query and document are encoded **separately**.

Then, during scoring, CoLBERT performs a **MaxSim operation (heart of CoLBert)**:

score(Q,D)=∑i=1mmaxjcos⁡(qi,dj)

Here’s what this means:

- For each **query token** qi​, find the **most similar document token** dj​.

- Aggregate these maxima across all query tokens (hence, it is a N query to M docs operation).


This “max over document tokens” simulates how each query concept finds its best representation in the document, like a “best local match per word”, this simulation was performed in weight space by attention in Cross-Encoder (resulting in inefficiency). This is **late interaction**, each token only interacts at scoring time, not during encoding.

Hence, CoLBERT saves enormous computation by **avoiding full cross-attention between every query and document token**.

## LLMs as Rerankers : From Matching to Meaning

At this point, our reranking journey has moved through layers of _perception_:

- From **derived reranking**, where we polish what we already have.

- To **hybrid reranking**, where we expand our horizons.

- To **CoLBERT**, which finds/simulates local meaning without losing efficiency.


But there’s one more leap; a leap from _recognition_ to _reasoning_. Traditional rerankers “match” texts, whereas LLM rerankers _understand_ them.

Imagine a query: “Which court ruled on the liability of the manufacturer in the Bhopal gas tragedy?” A bi-encoder might surface documents mentioning _Bhopal_, _court_, and _liability_. A cross-encoder might score the most linguistically similar passages highest.

But only an **LLM-based reranker** can reason: “This document mentions the Supreme Court judgment _holding_ the manufacturer liable.” or “This one discusses an _appeal_ but not the actual ruling.”

[![Using LLM's for Retrieval and Reranking — LlamaIndex - Build Knowledge  Assistants over your Enterprise Data](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!16tM!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F795fae47-7b17-4369-9939-26f80b289248_3272x934.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!16tM!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F795fae47-7b17-4369-9939-26f80b289248_3272x934.png)

If traditional rerankers are pattern detectors, LLM rerankers are _narrative interpreters_.

This becomes especially useful when:

- The query is **implicit** or **underspecified**.

- The documents contain **multi-hop reasoning** or **temporal** information.

- The notion of “relevance” depends on **intent** or **factual consistency**, not just lexical overlap.


### The Setup

At a structural level, reranking is simple:

ri=f(q,di)

where f is your scoring function, mapping query–document pairs to relevance scores.

When f becomes an **LLM**, the nature of f changes, as it becomes a _language reasoning process_ rather than a static function. You’re no longer computing a similarity;

you’re asking: _“Given the question, how strongly does this document support, answer, or contradict it?”_ Hence _,_ The reranking step becomes a _micro chain-of-thought task_.

Let’s formalize it (which eventually is just prompt engeineering).

Given query q and candidate documents {d1,d2,...,dK}, the LLM reranker performs:

si=LLM(Prompt(q,di))

The prompt could be as simple as:

_“Question: {q}\\nDocument: {d\_i}\\nIs this document relevant to the question? Answer:”_

The model outputs a probability (if you have open LLMs) or a discrete label (e.g., “Yes/No”) with closed LLMs like Gemini, Chatgpt, etc., which can be converted into a score.

In practice, one might use:

- **Logits from completion likelihood**

- **Softmax-normalized probabilities**

- **Pairwise preference scoring** (e.g., compare two docs and see which is preferred)


This makes reranking a _prompt-engineering + scoring aggregation_ problem. This combined with prompt optimization + feedback setup like DSPy becomes really powerful.

### Challenges with using LLMs as reranker

But, LLM reranking is still a young paradigm, and it comes with its own thorns:

1. **Latency :** Evaluating each document with an LLM can be slow.

2. **Cost :** Token-based billing makes reranking expensive for large K.

3. **Hallucination :** LLMs may invent reasoning chains to justify a wrong label.

4. **Evaluation drift :** Subjective notions of “relevance” vary with prompts or models.


In summary, If we step back, a pattern quietly emerges across all reranking methods, a continuum from _surface-level similarity_ to _deep contextual understanding_.

- **Bi-encoders** operate on _geometry_ : mapping meaning into a shared vector space.

- **Cross-encoders** add _interaction_ : letting query and document talk token-to-token per layer.

- **CoLBERT** balances both : local attention without global slowdown.

- **LLM rerankers** transcend matching altogether and they _reason_, _interpret_, and _judge_.


It’s a spectrum of cognition: from _pattern recognition_ → _context modeling_ → _semantic reasoning_.

And that progression hints at what’s next, reranking that moves _beyond text_, where “relevance” might depend not on words but on **images**, **sounds**, or **actions** in an agentic loop.

# 5\. Re-ranking Across Modalities

So far, our exploration of reranking has been largely textual: nodes, paragraphs, documents. Derived reranking polishes what’s retrieved, hybrid expands recall, CoLBERT adds token-level reasoning, and LLMs bring in semantic and logical judgment. But information comes in many forms like images, videos, audio, tabular data and the definition of “relevance” shifts subtly but crucially with each modality.

Reranking across modalities is about **understanding the nature of each data type**, deciding which signals matter, and aligning them with the query in a way that mirrors our earlier textual pipelines, but now across sensory or structured spaces.

### Images/Visual

**Low-Level Features:**

Historically, image retrieval relied on low-level descriptors: SIFT (, SURF, ORB, or color histograms. Conceptually, these are like **BM25 for text**, as they do not understand content semantically, but they capture _structural patterns_.

[![OpenCV: Introduction to SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3I7t!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe879d619-e97f-4c7d-9054-df623963359e_450x338.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3I7t!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe879d619-e97f-4c7d-9054-df623963359e_450x338.jpeg) SIFT as feature detector

For instance, ORB keypoints can help find documents containing similar logos, shapes, or repeated visual motifs. Derived reranking in this space can reorder candidates based on the number or quality of keypoint matches with the query image.

**High-Level/Semantic Features:**

Modern pipelines encode images with deep networks: ResNets, ViTs, or specialized embeddings like **CLIP or ColPali (extension to CoLBERT)**. These act like bi-encoders in text: the query and candidate images are embedded independently, and similarity is measured via cosine or dot product. Cross-encoder analogs exist too: visual cross-attention models can jointly consider the query image and candidate images, analogous to token-to-token interaction in CoLBERT.

[![An Overview of Late Interaction Retrieval Models: ColBERT, ColPali, and  ColQwen | Weaviate](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!98eW!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8bbbd092-08ab-465b-a4f0-0f0f72e4facd_1358x709.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!98eW!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8bbbd092-08ab-465b-a4f0-0f0f72e4facd_1358x709.jpeg) [source](https://weaviate.io/blog/late-interaction-overview)

Finally, Hybrid-like strategies can be applied here: combine low-level ORB-based retrieval (fast, broad, recall-oriented) with high-level embedding-based reranking (precision-oriented) and rank using RRF. The low-level step ensures we don’t miss visually similar candidates, while high-level embeddings capture semantic relevance. LLMs can also intervene when image metadata or captions exist, reasoning over context.

**But, there are few distinct issues:**

- Low-level features are brittle to noise, rotation, and illumination.

- High-level embeddings may conflate visually similar but semantically irrelevant images (e.g., a cat on a piano vs. a piano with no cat).


### Videos : Temporal + Spatial Dimensions

Video reranking introduces **time** as a new axis. Low-level features include ORB/SIFT keypoints in frames, motion vectors, or color histograms per frame. Derived reranking can reorder clips based on frame-level similarity scores.

High-level features leverage video encoders (e.g., **TimeSformer, VideoCLIP**) producing spatio-temporal embeddings. Bi-encoder style: embed query (text or video) and candidate clips separately; cross-encoder style: use temporal attention across query and candidate sequences. Hybrid reranking can fuse low-level frame features with high-level embeddings to balance recall and precision.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!vf8X!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F73754639-4819-4918-81e5-9053b88cb88f_2064x2128.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!vf8X!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F73754639-4819-4918-81e5-9053b88cb88f_2064x2128.png)

Dynamic retrieval here is especially important: initial retrieval might use a sparse set of keyframes (fast recall), then rerank top-K sequences using high-level embeddings or attention models. LLMs can also be used to reason over transcripts or captions for semantic relevance.

Issues here are:

- Frame-level low-level features can be noisy and miss temporal context.

- High-level embeddings may lose fine-grained temporal details (e.g., an important 2-second clip).

- Cross-encoder video reranking is extremely computationally expensive.


### Tabular/Structured Data

**Low-Level Features:**

For structured tabular data, low-level retrieval often relies on exact matches, keywords, or numeric proximity; essentially **BM25 analogs for tables**. For example, a query like _“Find tables with sales > 1M in 2024”_ may first retrieve candidates by matching column names (“sales”, “year”) and performing simple numeric filters.

Time-series data can also benefit from low-level feature extraction. Think of features like **peak detection, moving averages, autocorrelation, or Fourier coefficients** as these capture fundamental temporal patterns (though simplistic). A query such as _“Find time-series showing monthly revenue spikes in Q2”_ can first filter series that match these low-level patterns before applying semantic reranking.

**High-Level Features:**

Once candidate tables or series are retrieved, **embedding-based approaches** can refine relevance. Row-level or column-level embeddings (via models like **TabNet**, **TaBERT**, or temporal transformers for time-series) capture semantic structure, much like bi-encoders for text. Each row, column, or temporal segment can be represented as a vector, allowing similarity scoring between the query and candidates.

Cross-encoder equivalents model interactions between the query and the **entire table or series (using models like TimesNet, Timesformer, NBEATS, etc.)**, checking that the relational logic or temporal pattern aligns with the query.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!HOhM!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F791fd742-2466-41f7-8fe6-40445836cd1d_1876x2008.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!HOhM!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F791fd742-2466-41f7-8fe6-40445836cd1d_1876x2008.png)

Hybrid approaches can combine keyword matching (fast, broad recall) with embedding-based reranking (precision). Additionally, one can dynamically choose between row-level vs table-level embeddings depending on the query granularity, analogous to multi-granular node reranking in text.

_**But**, exact matches are brittle; embeddings can lose numeric precision or column semantics. Also the Cross-encoder approaches can be computationally heavy for large tables._

### Multi-Modal : Combining Modalities

Finally, consider **multi-modal reranking**: queries or candidates may span multiple modalities simultaneously. Examples:

- A query like “Find video clips of cats playing piano” requires **text + visual + audio reasoning**.

- A document could contain text descriptions, images, and video frames.


Here, strategies from earlier modalities combine:

1. **Hybrid retrieval across modalities**: separate low-level retrieval per modality, then fuse candidates.

2. **Derived reranking across embeddings**: high-level embeddings per modality feed into a reranker.

3. **Cross-modal attention / CoLBERT analogs**: cross-attend between modalities, e.g., text query attending to frames and audio.

4. **LLM-based multi-modal reasoning**: the final step can integrate captions, transcripts, and metadata, making semantic judgments across heterogeneous modalities.


Dynamic retrieval is essential: depending on query type or modality importance, the system may weight visual vs audio vs textual signals differently, analogous to weighting BM25 vs dense embeddings in hybrid textual reranking.

**Issues in Multi-Modal:**

- Alignment across modalities is hard, temporal misalignment or inconsistent granularity can hurt performance.

- Computation scales rapidly; precomputing embeddings per modality is crucial.

- Evaluation is tricky, as standard metrics rarely capture cross-modal relevance fully.

# 6\. Reranking Across Agents

Until now, reranking has focused on **information units**: text nodes, image frames, table rows, video clips, or audio segments. We’ve seen how derived, hybrid, CoLBERT, and LLM-based rerankers reorder candidates based on precision, recall, local alignment, and reasoning. But what happens when **the candidates themselves are outputs of independent systems or agents** that each interpret, generate, or summarize information differently?

This is where **agent-level reranking** enters: the task isn’t just “which document is relevant?” but “which agent’s output best addresses the query?” and sometimes, **how to combine multiple agents’ perspectives for a richer answer**.

### What Are Agents in This Context?

An agent is simply LLM + Memory + Tools, it eventually can be:

- An LLM fine-tuned for a specific domain.

- A retrieval system optimized for a particular modality.

- A reasoning module with specialized heuristics or tools.

- A multi-step pipeline producing summaries, translations, or recommendations.


[![LLM Agents | Prompt Engineering Guide](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Kcew!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc5ed9c20-c48d-43e4-9e3a-9150d7d5eaaa_927x618.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Kcew!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc5ed9c20-c48d-43e4-9e3a-9150d7d5eaaa_927x618.png)

Each agent is effectively an **independent node**, generating candidates with its own bias, knowledge, and scoring mechanism. Unlike traditional reranking, the “documents” here are **outputs from reasoning entities**, not just static data. Visually, imagine a **row of experts**, each holding a different colored folder representing their response. Some folders overlap, some contradict, some complement each other.

### Why Reranking Is Necessary Across Agents

Even the most sophisticated agents are imperfect:

- Two LLMs may produce conflicting summaries or answers.

- Multi-modal agents may disagree on which modality is most relevant.

- Agents specialized in precision may miss broader context, and vice versa.


Imagine each agent’s output as a **document in a stack of papers on a table**. The table is cluttered. Reranking is your hand sorting through: placing the most relevant on top for visual clarity, merging complementary notes, and discarding contradictions.

Reranking across agents allows us to:

1. **Select the best candidate** from a set of agent outputs.

2. **Fuse complementary outputs**, e.g., combining a high-precision textual answer with a high-recall visual summary.

3. **Resolve contradictions or conflicts**, leveraging meta-knowledge about agent reliability.


Conceptually, this is like **CoLBERT at the agent level**: instead of comparing token embeddings, we compare **agent outputs**, which may themselves be multi-modal or multi-step reasoning chains.

### Approaches for Agent-Level Reranking

**1\. Pointwise Scoring:**

Treat each agent output independently, checking for task/query alignment. To compute a score:

si=fθ(query,agenti’s output)

- fθ​ can be an LLM, a cross-encoder, or a scoring function trained to estimate correctness, completeness, or usefulness.

- Simple, parallelizable, works well when outputs are self-contained.


**2\. Pairwise Comparison:**

Compare outputs in pairs:

si,j=gθ(query,outputi,outputj)

- Useful for consistency and ranking outputs relative to each other.

- Captures nuances that single-output scoring may miss.


**3\. Listwise / Consensus:**

Consider all agent outputs together and produce a global ranking:

- Can leverage **voting schemes**, **weighted aggregation**, or **LLM reasoning over multiple outputs**.

- Aligns with hybrid retrieval philosophy: broad candidate exploration followed by precise reordering


### Challenges

- **Bias and reliability:** Agents vary in accuracy; reranker must account for this.

- **Diversity vs precision:** Top-scoring outputs may be redundant; need diversity-aware ranking.

- **Cross-modal, multi-agent fusion:** Complexity grows combinatorially when agents produce multi-modal outputs.

- **Evaluation metrics:** Traditional text metrics may fail; human evaluation or task-specific metrics are often required.

# 7\. Thoughts

- Reranking feels like _second-order retrieval_; not about “finding” information but “rethinking” it, similar to how reflection mechanisms in LLMs refine answers post-generation. The transition from CoLBERT to LLM-based rerankers mirrors a cognitive leap: from _matching tokens_ to _evaluating meaning_ is a shift from optics to semantics.

- Multi-agent reranking could evolve into _retrieval dialogues_ where different expert rerankers argue for or against results before convergence, mimicking human deliberation.

- “Efficiency” may soon be redefined not by FLOPs or latency but by _information compression_: how little reasoning a reranker can perform while preserving interpretive quality.

# 8\. Open Challenges & Research Directions

1. **Explainability in Reranking Decisions**

Rerankers, especially LLM-based ones, often act as black boxes; they can _tell_ us what’s most relevant but not _why_. Understanding their internal reasoning, attention shifts, and decision boundaries is crucial for trust, debugging, and transparency. Future systems might need _explainable scoring layers_ that justify reordering in natural language or visual cues.

2. **Dynamic Modality Weighting**

Cross-modal reranking still treats modalities as static participants; but queries are fluid. A question about “climate data visualization” should weigh spatial and visual context differently from “climate policy arguments.” Designing rerankers that dynamically shift modality importance based on query intent could lead to much more context-sensitive retrieval.

3. **Hierarchical Multi-Agent Pipelines**

As retrieval systems scale, a single reranker is too narrow a bottleneck. Imagine a hierarchy of specialized agents: one reasoning over images, another verifying sources, a third judging coherence, each producing intermediate rankings before a meta-reranker fuses them. This distributed reranking could resemble _committee-style cognition_, balancing specialization with synthesis.

4. **Learning to Rerank from Feedback Loops**

Most rerankers are trained once and frozen. But as users interact, click, or correct, the relevance landscape shifts. A long-term goal is _continual reranking_, a system that evolve as retrieval environments and user intent evolve, closing the feedback loop between inference and adaptation.

5. **Balancing Latency and Depth of Understanding**

There’s a persistent trade-off between fast approximate retrieval (dense/sparse) and deep, interpretive reranking (cross-encoder or LLM). Bridging this gap could mean partial reasoning like models that learn to think “just enough” before deciding, allocating computation adaptively based on query complexity (things like speculative decoding could be interesting here).

6. **Unified Representation Spaces for Cross-Model Reranking**

Different models encode relevance differently like text vs. vision, bi-encoder vs. LLM. Aligning their embeddings into a coherent space for shared scoring remains an open challenge. This touches on _cross-embedding alignment_ and _semantic calibration_ crucial for integrating specialized rerankers into larger ecosystems.

7. **Trust and Bias Calibration**

Rerankers (especially Bi-encoder) can amplify biases present in embeddings or initial retrievals. A calibrated reranker would understand its own uncertainty knowing when to defer, abstain, or expose ambiguous rankings instead of over-confidently reordering them.

# 9\. Conclusion

And with that, we close this exploration into **reranking**, the layer that quietly transforms search into understanding. What began as a mechanical pipeline of query → retrieve → generate now feels more like a conversation between memory and attention, where each retrieved piece is not just _found_ but _re-evaluated_.

We began by revisiting the **conventional RAG pipeline**, where retrieval served as the engine and generation as the voice. Yet, as we saw, the cracks appeared when semantics overpowered structure like “dog” and “cat” sat too close in embedding space despite worlds of difference in context. Then came the intuition: maybe the problem wasn’t retrieval at all; but the lack of a _second thought_ and that’s where reranking stepped in.

From there, we moved through the **mathematics of ranking**, from classical probabilistic formulations to modern-day transformation functions and similarity metrics as the tools that shape how models perceive closeness and meaning. We saw how reranking is less about rearranging lists, and more about reshaping _relationships_.

Then came the **methods** where we saw the derived and hybrid rerankers; where we realized that derived reranking aims for _precision_, focusing on refining the top-K, while hybrid systems expand toward _recall_, blending different retrievers and fusion schemes. Between bi-encoders, cross-encoders, and the elegant middle ground carved by **ColBERT**, we saw reranking evolve into a spectrum of efficiency, expressivity, and granularity. And when **LLMs entered the frame**, reranking started to look a lot like reasoning (contextual, adaptive, and deeply semantic).

The journey extended beyond text. We then saw how reranking manifests across **modalities** with image reranking moving from ORB and SIFT toward ColPali-like vision-language fusions, how tabular reranking encodes structure rather than semantics, and how audio and video rerankers must weigh time and space over static similarity. And then, in the most dynamic sense, we touched on **agents** where reranking is not just between data and query, but between thoughts, actions, and outputs of different systems negotiating shared intent.

By the end, reranking no longer felt like a post-process, it felt like the _judgment phase_ of intelligence. The moment where perception meets evaluation. It’s the bridge between retrieval and reasoning, between knowing and choosing.

In that light, reranking might not remain a small optimization layer for long. It could become the **cognitive/second-thought layer** of multi-agent and multimodal systems one that constantly re-orders context, relevance, and truth in real time. Because sometimes, intelligence isn’t about retrieving the right answer; it’s about learning how to _reconsider_ the ones we already have.

# Beyond Retrieval: Ensembling Cross-Encoders and GPT Rerankers with LLMs for Biomedical QA

Notebook for the BioASQ Lab at CLEF 2025

Shashank Verma1,\*,†, Fengyi Jiang1,† and Xiangning Xue1,†

1Georgia Institute of Technology, North Ave NW, Atlanta, GA 30332

# Abstract

Biomedical semantic question answering rooted in information retrieval can play a crucial role in keeping up to date with vast, rapidly evolving and ever-growing biomedical literature. A robust system can help researchers, healthcare professionals and even layman users access relevant knowledge grounded in evidence. The BioASQ 2025 Task13b Challenge serves as an important benchmark, offering a competitive platform for advancement of this space. This paper presents the methodologies and results from our participation in this challenge where we built a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system that can answer biomedical questions by retrieving relevant PubMed documents and snippets to generate answers. For the retrieval task, we generated dense embeddings from biomedical articles for initial retrieval, and applied an ensemble of finetuned cross-encoders and large language models (LLMs) for re-ranking to identify top relevant documents. Our solution achieved an $\\mathbf { M A P @ 1 0 }$ of 0.1581, placing 10th on the leaderboard for the retrieval task. For answer generation, we employed few-shot prompting of instruction-tuned LLMs. Our system achieved macro-F1 score of 0.95 for yes/no questions (rank 12), Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) of 0.64 for factoid questions (rank 1), mean-F1 score of 0.63 for list questions (rank 5), and ROUGE-SU4 F1 score of 0.29 for ideal answers (rank 11).

# Keywords

Biomedical question answering, Information Retrieval (IR), Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), Dense Retrieval, Re-Ranker, Large Language Model (LLM), Semantic Question Answering, Prompt Engineering

# 1\. Introduction

Answering biomedical questions with precise, well supported responses requires intensive searching, reading and synthesizing information from dozens of research articles - a time consuming task demanding both domain expertise and contextual understanding. It poses unique challenges due to domain-specific jargon and compositional question structure. Solving this problem will enable access to an accurate biomedical assistant for researchers and clinicians, supporting their decision-making and work efficiency and could even open doors for access to general public for self education and to help fight biomedical misinformation. BioASQ Task 13b Biomedical Semantic QA \[1\] describes this exact challenge, dividing it into two phases: Phase A is a retrieval task that identifies the most relevant list of documents and snippets for the given question, while Phase B focuses on generating both a formatted exact answer and a natural language ideal answer using the documents & snippets as context.

The BioASQ challenge (Nentidis et al. \[2\]) has been continuously evolving to advance biomedical question answering, and we are participating in its 13th edition. We were provided a BioASQ-QA dataset \[3\] with 5,389 questions, each accompanied with gold responses for most relevant documents, snippets, exact answers, and ideal answers that were curated by field experts. The number of gold documents and snippets varied but were generally in the order of tens (Fig. 1). Questions were divided into four types as shown in Fig. 1: yes/no $( \\mathrm { n } { = } 1 , 4 5 9 )$ ), factoid $\\scriptstyle ( \ n = 1 , 6 0 0 )$ , list $\_ { ( \\mathrm { n = 1 } , 0 4 7 ) }$ , and summary $\_ { ( \\mathrm { n = 1 } , 2 8 3 ) }$ . Question types define the format of exact answers: “yes” or “no” for yes/no questions; factoid questions expect a ranked list of alternative correct answers ordered by confidence, whereas list questions require a complete set of items without ranking. In addition to the exact answers, each of the question types also contain an ideal answer which is a natural language response to the question.

![](https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-4038/images/a6bbdb73046373a0a72fcea6645eeae0562789efc4ca7be6110206fe748e259f.jpg)

Figure 1: Distribution of question types in BioASQ training data (left) and number of golden documents & snippets per question (right).

In this paper, we present our automated Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system, which aims to solve this problem. While prior systems have largely relied on sparse retrieval using BM25 \[4\], which rely on word matching or entity based searching through PubMed API, our approach utilizes modern dense retrieval techniques and neural re-rankers with advanced LLM-based generation, allowing for strong performance evidenced by consistent top10 placement in the leaderboard across phases and question types. In summary, our work makes the following contributions:

1. We built a dense retrieval system using bge-large-en embeddings on the full PubMed corpus, significantly improving document recall.
2. We designed an ensemble of finetuned cross-encoders and GPT-based re-rankers to maximize $\\mathbf { M A P @ 1 0 }$ for retrieved documents.
3. We implemented a few-shot prompting pipeline with instruction-tuned LLMs to generate both exact and ideal answers.

# 2\. Related Work

# 2.1. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has emerged as a pivotal framework in natural language processing, particularly for enhancing the performance of large language models on knowledge-intensive tasks. The seminal work by Lewis et al \[5\], introduced this paradigm, demonstrating how combining retrieval-based and generation-based approaches can improve accuracy by grounding model outputs in external documents. This approach is especially relevant for domains requiring up-to-date and domain-specific knowledge, such as biomedical question and answering. Subsequent work by Izacard et al \[6\] further refined RAG by introducing Fusion-in-Decoder (FiD), which enhances generation by aggregating information from multiple retrieved documents.

# 2.2. Vector Databases for Scalable Search

Storing and querying large sets of embeddings, requires scalable and efficient data structures. Malkov et al\[7\] introduced Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) algorithm and provided the foundation of many vector database implementations, offering logarithmic complexity scaling for similarity searches. Johnson et al\[8\] further explored billion-scale similarity search, emphasizing GPU acceleration. Additionally, Annoy by Bernhardsson \[9\] offers an alternative ANN approach with tree-based indexing, though we prioritize HNSW for its balance of speed and accuracy.

# 2.3. Retrieval with Bi-Encoders and Cross-Encoders

Efficient and accurate retrieval is central to RAG pipeline. Common ranking methods include traditional statistical models such as BM25 \[4\], which rely on word matching, and more parameterized deep learning models like transformers based cross-encoders and bi-encoders, examples including PubMedBERT \[10\], MiniLM \[11\]. Bi-encoders, such as Sentence-BERT (Reimers and Gurevych \[12\]), encode queries and documents independently into dense vectors, enabling efficient similarity searches over large datasets. However, bi-encoders often trade precision for speed. Rosa et al\[13\] demonstrated the superiority of cross-encoders in zero-shot retrieval tasks while Nogueira and Cho \[14\] explored their use in passage re-ranking with BERT. Retrieving large number of documents with a bi-encoder and re-ranking to the top-k with a cross-encoder mirrors strategies evaluated in the BEIR benchmark by Thakur et al\[15\].

# 2.4. LLMs for Re-ranking

Large Language Models (LLMs) are state of the art in many natural language processing tasks and have been employed in various aspects of Information Retrieval including passage re-ranking. Recent work by Ma et al. \[16\] and Pradeep et al. \[17\] has shown that LLMs are able to perform zero-shot listwise document re-ranking leveraging their unparalleled understanding of natural language and reasoning capabilities, somewhat bypassing the need for domain-specific fine-tuning.

# 2.5. Fine-Tuning Domain-Specific Language Models

Luo et al \[18\] introduced BioGPT with domain-specific pre-training on 15 million PubMed abstracts which makes it well-suited for biomedical text generation. It can be adapted efficiently using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) by Hu et al \[19\], which reduces the number of trainable parameters by introducing low-rank updates to pre-trained weights. This parameter-efficient method mitigates the computational constraints we encountered, such as memory limitations, while maintaining performance.

Complementary approaches like AdapterFusion by Pfeiffer et al\[20\] offer modular fine-tuning across tasks, though we favor LoRA for its simplicity and compatibility with BioGPT. Lee et al\[21\] also highlight the value of domain-specific pre-training with BioBERT, reinforcing the importance of tailoring models to biomedical contexts.

# 2.6. Few-Shot Learning with Large Language Models

Few-shot prompting using instruction-tuned models like GPT-4o-turbo \[22\] and Mistral-7B-Instruct$\\mathrm { v } 0 . 3$ \[23\] leverages in-context learning, a concept popularized by Brown et al \[24\] with GPT-3, where models generate outputs based on a few prompt examples. Wei et al. \[25\] extended this with chainof-thought prompting, improving reasoning in complex tasks. Ateia and Kruschwitz \[26\] developed frameworks for structured answer generation in specialized domains.

# 3\. Methodology

# 3.1. Phase A - Indexing & Retrieval

To address the limitations of PubMed API’s keyword-based retrieval and improve recall, we built a custom index powered by dense vector search.

# 3.1.1. Dataset Preparation: PubMed 2025 Baseline

We downloaded the full PubMed 2025 Baseline \[27\], containing approximately 39 million records, including both article metadata and abstracts. The initial corpus was highly heterogeneous, with a subset of articles missing abstracts. Since abstracts are critical for semantic retrieval and question answering, we performed an initial preprocessing step to remove the documents with empty or missing abstracts, de-duplicated documents and filtered out the corrupted records. We then parsed the XML to extract the PMID, title and abstract \[27\]. After filtering, the resulting corpus contained ${ \\approx } 3 4$ million high-quality abstracts.

# 3.1.2. Embedding Generation: Bi-Encoder Model

For dense semantic indexing, we employed a bi-encoder architecture, wherein documents and queries are encoded independently into vector representations, and similarity is computed via a simple metric such as cosine similarity.

We selected the bge-large-en model, a state-of-the-art bi-encoder trained for English retrieval tasks, due to its large model capacity (1024-dim embeddings) and open-source availability. Each PubMed abstract was tokenized and encoded into a fixed-length 1024-dimensional embedding vector with care to truncate the abstracts to model’s maximum token limit of 512, if necessary.

# 3.1.3. Vector Databases for Semantic Search

The full set of embeddings was stored in a vector database optimized for large-scale approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search. During retrieval, given a user query, the query was similarly embedded and the top-K most similar documents were retrieved based on cosine similarity in the embedding space.

Initially, we explored using fully managed cloud-based deployment like Pinecone, but ultimately discarded it due to its high cost \[28\]. We finally settled on using a local Qdrant deployment \[29\] which allowed us to gain full fine-grained control over our index while saving the hosting cost of Pinecone.

# 3.2. Phase A - Document & Snippet Re-ranking

In a typical Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system, the quality of the retrieved content as context directly influences the accuracy and relevance of the generated responses. With a high-quality index in place, we can retrieve the top 10 documents and snippets by directly querying the index using the question embedded with the same bge-large-en model. However, as we discussed before, retrieving a large pool of documents followed by a re-ranking of those documents leads to better results \[30\].

Due to time constraints, we weren’t able to replicate our document retrieval & re-ranking setup as demonstrated in Fig. 2 for snippets. Across all systems, we used the same snippet retrieval strategy (which was the predecessor of all future strategies).

![](https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-4038/images/48ba0d7f0ca1db54c5950a41c448b40e3e63b3f524efdcbda4c05d962f61dfa3.jpg)

Figure 2: Architecture of the best performing system for Phase A. We use bge-large-en for creating our index and perform ensembled re-ranking to get the top-10 most relevant documents for a query.

# 3.2.1. Cross Encoders for Re-ranking

In our systems, we retrieve top-1k documents and then apply a re-ranking step to select the final top-10 documents. Bi-encoders embed question and document independently and compute similarity based on their embeddings which is the secret to their efficiency but also doesn’t allow them to exploit the interaction between the question and the document. This is addressed by using cross-encoders which jointly process the question and candidate document pairs.

Due to slower speed of cross-encoders, the two-stage hybrid approach of bi-encoders to maximize recall with top-1k retrieval followed by cross-encoders to maximize $\\mathrm { M A P @ 1 0 }$ in the final top-10 documents is the optimal approach balancing accuracy, performance, and computational cost.

# 3.2.2. Finetuning Cross Encoders

Every dataset and domain has certain nuances that are unique to it, which means that a general purpose model cannot exploit them. This is where a model finetuned on the domain’s datasets can outperform an out-of-the-box model. Since we had the BioASQ-QA dataset provided by the competition, we finetuned a few cross encoder models to learn the intricacies of PubMed knowledge base and how the field experts perceive them.

We stratified the dataset on question to split for train, val and test, to make sure that the questions evaluated on the validation and test set were never seen by the model during training. Positive examples were created using the golden documents and negative examples were generated by querying the index and removing the golden documents. These served as hard negatives for the model since they were somewhat relevant to the question, allowing the model to learn the fine line between somewhat relevant and truly relevant. Training dataset was prepared as question-document pair as input and a label of $0 / 1$ denoting whether the document was in the golden set for the question or not. The model was tasked with predicting the label given a question-document pair using a binary cross entropy loss. Evaluation and test data were prepared as tuples of question, all\_documents and golden\_documents, letting the model apply re-ranking on all\_documents to select the top-10 and be evaluated on metrics like MAP (mean average precision) which is what our competition was going to use on the leaderboard. We didn’t keep a minimum relevance threshold for the re-ranker output, and always selected the top-10 most relevant candidates.

Finally, we experimented with some dataset variations:

• Equal ratio of positive and negative examples: Ultimately discarded, since in the real application, we want to apply re-ranking to 1k documents to get top-10 which means positive and negative examples shouldn’t be equal.

• Discarding older questions from training: This was done with the rationale that there is an inevitable data drift with any temporally collected data. Models trained on recent data could better inform the future predictions. This turned out to be true in our case and we used the model trained only on last few years’ data.

# 3.2.3. LLMs for Re-ranking

LLMs understand the nuances of a text better than any language models. With that in mind, we experimented with using LLMs like gpt-4o for the re-ranking task. We explored two approaches:

• Prompt with the question-candidate pair and ask it to assign a relevance score. Then return the top 10 most relevant documents.

• Prompt with the question and all the top-30 candidate documents and ask it to return the reordered list of top-10 documents. In this scenario, we used the top-30 from applying the finetuned cross-encoder on the retrieved top-1k.

The first approach resulted in lower $\\mathbf { M A P @ 1 0 }$ compared to finetuned cross-encoder re-ranker. However, the second approach led to a sizable improvement.

# 3.2.4. Ensembling

We had two re-ranking systems: a) System1 was using finetuned cross encoder to get top-30 documents from 1k retrieved candidates, and b) System2 used finetuned cross-encoder to get to top-30 and gpt-4o prompting to further refine to top-10. We explored a couple of ways of combining the two systems:

• Nomination-based approach: First 6 from System1 and remaining 4 from System2. • Weighted combination of scores: A weighted summation of both system’s documents. Grid search was employed to find the best weights.

Weighted Ensembling gave us the best MAP of all the systems. The final architecture of our best solution using weighted ensembling for Phase A is shown in Fig. 2.

# 3.3. Phase B System: Answering Generation with Retrieved Data

In Phase B, we focused on generating answers using few-shot prompting of instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs), leveraging snippets retrieved in Phase A. Specifically, GPT-4o-turbo and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 models were used, implementing a variety of prompting templates designed to effectively guide the answer generation. While we also conducted experiments with fine-tuning BioGPT with task-specific heads, these yielded less competitive results compared to our prompting strategy; thus, detailed fine-tuning outcomes are omitted here but will be publicly available on our GitHub repository to support reproducibility and transparency.

![](https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-4038/images/b2694f3fb0908877b58702298cbc7e09f9baa9f60b40d124d291be816dc8e1b2.jpg)

Figure 3: Overall Prompt Template Structure. Template texts wrapped in ${ }$ are subject to change according to styles and questions.

![](https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-4038/images/cf6ab710315b5a0b1d2babbb28c2a6edff0c46ab3ab87b21524885970f3d3d58.jpg)

Figure 4: Query Templates for exact and ideal answers.

We experimented with two primary dimensions in our prompting strategy:

1. Number of Few-Shot Examples: We tested using either a single example (1-shot) or ten examples (10-shots) as contextual demonstrations, corresponding to $n = 1$ or 10 in Fig. 3. The examples were drawn from the training set as snippets-question-answer triplets to guide the model in generating appropriate responses.

Answer Formatting Template 2 (showing key changes from Template 1)

# List:

- Answers should be based on the passage content, but you may supplement with your own knowledge if necessary.
- Prefer the shortest, cleanest, and most direct entry cut from the Passage that -accurately answer the question.
- Note that all phrases, even not complete, are related to the question.

# Factoid:

- Each element must be a complete answer to the question. Do not include synonyms or duplicate meanings. Avoid acronyms unless the full name is unavailable.

  Avoid overly long phrases, redundant details, or overly specific descriptions unless necessary. - When multiple numerical answers are given (e.g., different rates, frequencies, or ranges across populations), merge them into a single range or compact expression if appropriate, instead of listing them separately.
- The returned entity names must not be synonyms of each other.

# Summary:

- Prefer answers of only combining direct phrases or sentences from the Passage. You may add minimal connecting words (such as “and”, “which”, “that”, “because”, “thus”) to make the answer grammatically correct, but do not paraphrase the original wording unless necessary.

Figure 5: Answer Formatting Templates. Template 1 was presented in Ateia & Kruschwitz’s published work \[26\] and thus omitted.

2. Prompts Templates Design: Each prompt varied along two core components: the Query Template, which defined how few-shot examples and questions were presented, and the Answer Formatting Template, which instructed the model on the expected format of question-specific responses. Below we describe the distinct styles we implemented:

• Query Templates: As shown in Fig. 4, Template 1 generates prompts for all exact answers and ideal answers independent of the question id. While in Template 2, we integrate the system-generated exact answers as a hint for non-summary-type ideal answers. Additionally, we modified the list type example: in Template 1, only a single correct list item for each entry was shown as example, while in Template 2, we show the entire golden answer. • Answer Formatting Templates: Template 1 was adapted from the instruction style proposed by Ateia & Kruschwitz \[26\], specifying concise, type-aware answers consistent with BioASQ guidelines. In Fig. 5, we illustrate the key modifications introduced in Template 2, which were designed to address observed issues in system outputs—such as redundancy, synonym repetition, or incomplete phrasing—especially for list and factoid types.

Combining different Query and Answer Formatting Templates, we defined three distinct prompt styles used in our experiments:

• Style 1: Query Template $1 +$ Answer Formatting Template 1.

• Style 2: Query Template $2 +$ Answer Formatting Template 1.

• Style 3: Query Template $2 +$ Answer Formatting Template 2.

# 4\. Results

# 4.1. Phase A: Retrieval

The retrieval comparison method evaluates the performance of a vector embedding database against PubMed’s retrieval system using BioASQ dataset, which contains 5,389 question - PMID gold standard pairs. We tested retrieving top 10, 100, 1000, and 10,000 documents from the vector database and measuring the counts of true positives as shown in Table 1

# 5\. Discussion

Our custom Qdrant Vector Database, utilizing the bge-large-en bi-encoder, significantly outperformed the PubMed Query API in retrieving relevant documents. As shown in Table 1, all Recall@N values (e.g., Recall@ $) 1 0 = 0 . 2 3$ vs. 0.10, Recall@1k $= 0 . 5 6$ vs. 0.23) demonstrate the superiority of dense-vector search over traditional keyword-based retrieval. This advantage stems from the bi-encoder’s ability to capture semantic relationships in biomedical texts.

Initial retrieval of 1k candidates followed by re-ranking with an ensemble of cross-encoders and GPT-based re-rankers, further enhanced the retrieval performance as shown in Table 2. While retrieving top10 documents from index with no re-ranker gets us an $\\mathrm { M A P @ 1 0 }$ of 0.1895 only, retrieving 1k followed by re-ranking via finetuned cross encoder achieves an $\\mathrm { M A P @ 1 0 }$ of 0.4337 (more than doubled). Applying ensemble re-rankers takes us all the way to 0.4551 on our test set. This reflects the effectiveness of combining bi-encoders for high recall with cross-encoders and LLMs for precise re-ranking, allowing the system to identify the most relevant documents from a large pool. It is interesting to note that each next stage is as much or more accurate as well as more expensive on the IR task. Bi-encoders are the most efficient, seamlessly searching through millions of documents to get us an initial 1k candidates. Cross-encoders jointly look at query and candidate pair making them slow albeit more accurate, which is why they are applied on only the smaller pool of retrieved 1k documents. Using LLMs as re-rankers takes more time to re-rank and is much more costly per question but probably slightly more accurate than cross-encoders, which is why they are employed on the top30 cross-encoder re-ranked documents only.

An interesting observation in the re-ranking stage (Table 2) is that models like jina-reranker-v2-basemultilingual and bge-reranker-large are much larger models with 278M and 560M params respectively compared to the best performing model ms-marco-MiniLM-L12 which has only 33.4M params. This reveals the fact that the pre-training of each model and the model’s architecture lead to models specializing in different aspects and tasks.

As a future followup, we would like to explore using language models to reformulate the query for improved retrievals. Additionally, increasing the retrieval from 1k to 2k showed improvement (System2 had better score than System1), which means we can further optimize the configuration for our best system by retrieving more documents from the index.

For Phase B, we also experimented with model fine-tuning using BioGPT. As a decoder-only model trained to generate continuous text based on prior context, BioGPT inherently outputs free-form text. For instance, when responding to a yes/no question, it frequently provided verbose answers instead of direct “yes” or “no” responses. To rectify this, we implemented task-specific heads on top of the pre-trained model: a linear layer projecting hidden states into binary outputs for yes/no questions and a span-prediction head for identifying the start and end indices of answers within provided snippets for factoid questions. Due to limited training data and computational constraints, we anticipated limited performance improvements. Additionally, memory constraints and unstable gradient descent posed challenges. Despite resolving stability issues, fine-tuned methods consistently showed limited performance: yes/no predictions defaulted to “yes,” and factoid responses frequently were incomplete. Consequently, results presented herein focus solely on prompting strategies, though detailed fine-tuning outcomes are publicly available in our GitHub repository.

Returning to our submitted prompting-based Phase B systems, although these systems achieved perfect scores for yes/no questions in our internal experiments, the real submission batches continued to hold the success in batch1 and batch2 but dropped a bit for batch4. This discrepancy indicates a critical limitation of our evaluation strategy: sampled evaluation questions may not comprehensively represent the complexity and variability encountered in real-world questions, masking shortcomings in our prompts for yes/no questions. Moreover, certain questions consistently underperformed across all tested systems, often due to overly long or repetitive snippets that diluted contextual relevance. These observations suggest future research directions such as introducing snippet filtering or prioritization methods to select more diverse and informative contexts, potentially enhancing both exact and ideal answer generation.

# 6\. Conclusion

In this paper, we discussed our participation in the BioASQ’s Semantic Question Answering challenge. We developed a RAG system for biomedical queries which retrieves from a huge PubMed index (O(10M) documents). We have shown that our custom local Qdrant Vector Database with Bi-Encoder performs significantly better than using PubMed Query API. The retrieval performance was further improved by employing a two-stage re-ranker ensemble. We got competitive results on the leaderboard at rank 10 and we believe that this tiered approach is the way to go for future improvements.

In answer generation phase, we were able to top the leaderboard for factoid questions and be competitive for all other question types (generally in top10), showing that for generating real natural language responses, instruction tuned LLMs are extremely competitive.

A Biomedical Semantic Question Answering system has huge implications in the real-world. This can help medical researchers in the field as well as layman users in answering their queries with authoritative sources to back them up. It can also help mitigate medical misinformation by applying to fact-check various claims on the internet.
